title: How to use Google Pay in Nigeria
summary: Google Pay is live in Nigeria. See which banks and cards work, how to set it up, and where you can actually pay with it. Get started.
body_markdown:
Google Pay launched in Nigeria on 28 October 2026, through the Google Wallet app on Android. Google’s current list covers eligible cards from five banks: FirstBank, GTBank, Providus Bank, UBA, and Zenith Bank, mostly Mastercard. Verve, AfriGO, and cards from banks like OPay, Moniepoint, Kuda, and PalmPay are not on it, and contactless terminals remain limited.


Whether tapping works depends on three things: your card, your phone, and the terminal. This guide takes them in that order, then covers what to do if your card is not supported.


## Does Google Pay work in Nigeria?


Yes. Google launched Google Wallet, including Google Pay, in Nigeria on 28 October 2026 for Android and Wear OS users. Google says it lets you pay by tapping in stores, in apps, and online, using a card stored on your phone.


The two names cause confusion, so here is the difference. Google Wallet is the app. It holds your payment cards, and it can also hold loyalty cards, event tickets, and boarding passes. Google Pay is the payment function inside it, the part that passes your card to a terminal or a checkout page. You install one app, add a card, and pay with Google Pay.


Unfortunately, Google Pay won’t work for everyone. Three things have to line up:


- **Your card:** It has to be on Google's list, and your bank decides whether a given card works.
- **Your phone:** It has to run Android and have a screen lock. Tapping in stores also needs NFC.
- **The place you are paying.** An online shop has to offer Google Pay, and a physical shop needs a contactless-enabled terminal.


The next section covers the first of these: the banks and cards.


## Nigerian banks and cards that work with Google Pay


The table below follows[Google’s Nigeria payment methods page](https://support.google.com/wallet/answer/12059326?hl=en&co=GENIE.CountryCode%3DNG) , as at the time of publishing.


\\begin{table}\[\] \\begin{tabular}{ll} \\textbf{Bank} & \\textbf{Supported cards} \\\\ First Bank of Nigeria & Mastercard debit \\\\ Guaranty Trust Bank (GTBank) & Mastercard debit and prepaid \\\\ Providus Bank & Mastercard credit, debit, and prepaid \\\\ United Bank for Africa (UBA) & Mastercard credit, debit, and prepaid; Visa prepaid \\\\ Zenith Bank & Mastercard credit, debit, and prepaid \\end{tabular} \\end{table}


An account at a listed bank is not enough. Google has stressed that your bank decides whether its cards work with Google Wallet. The card network (Mastercard or Visa) and the card type (debit, credit, or prepaid) both count. A bank that issues Mastercard and Verve cards may support one but not the other, so find the row for your bank, then check the network and card type you hold. Both are usually shown on the card itself or in your banking app.


**What is not supported:**


- Verve cards. Google currently only supports Mastercard and Visa.
- AfriGO cards.
- Cards from OPay, Moniepoint, Kuda, and PalmPay. None of these providers appears on the list.
- Visa debit cards from the listed banks. Visa appears only as a prepaid card at UBA.


If your card is not covered, the section below on unsupported cards outlines your options.


## How to set up Google Pay in Nigeria


You need an Android phone, a screen lock, and a card from the table above. For tapping in stores, the phone also needs NFC. Google Wallet generally asks for a recent version of Android, so update your phone first if it is running old software.


1. **Set a screen lock.** Wallet needs a PIN, pattern, password, or fingerprint before it stores a payment card.
2. **Install Google Wallet.** Download it from the Google Play Store and open it.
3. **Add the card.** Tap Add to Wallet, then Payment card, then New credit or debit card.
4. **Enter the card details.** Scan the card with the camera, or type the number, expiry date, and CVV.
5. **Accept the terms and verify.** Your bank may send an SMS code or ask you to confirm in its app. Complete this step to activate the card.
6. **Set a default.** Open Wallet settings and choose the card you want Google Pay to use first.
7. **Check NFC.** In your phone's settings, search for NFC and switch it on if you plan to tap in stores.


If the verification message does not arrive, or the card is declined, call the number on the back of the card. Google's page says to contact your bank when a card cannot be set up for mobile payments.


Virtual cards go in the same way. Grey's guide on[how to add a virtual card to Apple Pay or Google Pay](https://grey.co/blog/virtual-card-apple-pay-google-pay) covers it in more detail.


## How to set up Google Pay with your Grey card


*Writer flag, remove before publishing: these steps come from Grey's published guide and have not been walked on a device. Confirm which Grey card types are eligible and whether a Nigerian Google account can add one, then add screenshots.*


If your bank card is not on Google's list, a Grey virtual dollar card is another card you can try in Google Wallet. Grey's guide says its virtual cards can be added to Google Wallet on Android, and that Google Pay accepts virtual debit cards on the Mastercard and Visa networks as long as the issuer supports it. Google decides which countries and cards Wallet supports, so availability can vary by region.


**What you need:** an active, funded Grey virtual card and an Android phone with a screen lock. A frozen or expired card, or one with a $0 balance, can fail verification.


1. In the Grey app, go to Cards, tap your virtual card, and copy the card number, expiry date, and CVV.
2. Open Google Wallet, tap Add to Wallet, then Payment card.
3. Tap New credit or debit card and enter the details.
4. Tap Save. Google checks the card with the issuer.
5. Accept the terms and complete the verification step. This may be an SMS code, an email link, or a confirmation in the Grey app.
6. Open Wallet settings and set the card as your default payment method.


Adding a card to Google Pay is free. Any fees come from the card issuer.


**What it is good for**


A Grey virtual card holds US dollars, so it suits payments priced in dollars:


- International online checkouts that show Google Pay at the payment step.
- Subscriptions billed abroad in dollars, such as software and streaming.
- Spending when your Nigerian bank card is not on Google's list.


It is a dollar card, so it does not replace a naira bank card for everyday spending in Nigerian shops. For that, a card on Google's list is the simpler fit.


You can[get a Grey virtual card](https://grey.co/cards) from the app, and[fund your card from a USD balance](https://grey.co/foreign-accounts) so it is ready when you need to pay.

## Where you can actually use Google Pay in Nigeria


Online checkout is the realistic use for most people right now. Tapping in stores is possible, but only at terminals that support it, and those are still uncommon.


**Online.** Paystack has offered Google Pay at checkout for Nigerian merchants since September 2026, and Interswitch's payment gateway supports it too. Each merchant has to switch it on, so you will not see it at every shop. A business turns it on in its Paystack dashboard, and[Paystack's help page](https://support.paystack.com/en/articles/10458754) lists the requirements. Paystack supports Visa and Mastercard for Google Pay, and the option appears only when your device, browser, card, and Wallet setup all support it. If a checkout shows no Google Pay button, the cause is usually one of those four, or the merchant has not enabled it.


**In apps.** Some apps offer Google Pay at the payment step. The same rule applies: the app has to support it, and your card has to be on Google's list.


**In stores.** Tapping needs two things: a phone with NFC and a terminal with contactless enabled. Many point-of-sale terminals in use today lack the hardware, and contactless is still a very small share of payments in Nigeria. Even at a terminal that accepts taps, your bank's fraud systems have to recognise the payment, or it may be declined.


**How to tell whether a terminal will work:**


- Look for the contactless symbol, four curved lines, on the terminal or its screen.
- Ask the cashier before the bill is settled: "Does this take tap to pay?"
- Unlock your phone, switch NFC on, and hold the back of the phone close to the reader for a few seconds.
- If nothing happens after two or three tries, pay another way.


A practical rule is to use Google Pay online first and treat tapping in stores as a bonus where the terminal supports it. Keep a physical card or cash with you either way.


## If your card is not supported


Your card may not be on Google's list. What you do next depends on what you wanted to pay for.

A merchant that accepts your card takes it at checkout without Wallet.Pay in dollars at international shops and subscriptionsA virtual dollar cardIt is built for dollar payments, not for everyday naira spending.


**Waiting for your bank.** The list was shorter at launch than it is now, so more banks and card types may follow. There is no published timetable, so do not plan around it.


**Switching to a supported card type.** If you bank with one of the five listed banks but hold a Verve or Visa card, ask whether the bank can issue a Mastercard debit or prepaid card. Then check that exact type against Google's list. This keeps you paying from your naira account.


**Using a virtual dollar card.** For international online payments, Google Pay is rarely the blocker, because you can type a card's details at any checkout that accepts it. A virtual dollar card gives you a dollar card number for those payments. To compare your choices, read about[free virtual dollar cards](https://grey.co/blog/free-virtual-dollar-cards) and[how to get a virtual dollar card in Nigeria](https://grey.co/blog/virtual-dollar-card-nigeria) . A dollar card does not replace a naira bank card at home. If you also need to move money between Nigeria and another country, you can[send and receive money in Nigeria](https://grey.co/send-money/nigeria) with Grey.


*Fees apply to Grey virtual cards, including a one-time $5 creation fee, and currency conversion can add cost. See*[grey.co/pricing](https://grey.co/pricing) *for current fees.*


## Frequently asked questions


### Does Google Pay work in Nigeria?


Yes. Google launched Google Wallet, including Google Pay, in Nigeria on 28 October 2026 for Android and Wear OS. It works only with cards on Google's list, and only at online shops and terminals that support it.


### Which banks support Google Pay in Nigeria?


Google's list currently shows First Bank of Nigeria, GTBank, Providus Bank, UBA, and Zenith Bank. Support depends on the specific card, mostly Mastercard debit, credit, or prepaid. The table in this guide shows the exact types for each bank, and the list can change.


### Why was my card rejected?


The most likely cause is that the card is not on Google's list, or your bank has not enabled that card type. Verve and AfriGO cards are not supported. Other causes are a missing screen lock, an unfinished verification step, or a bank fraud check that blocked the payment. Call the number on the back of your card and ask the bank.


### Can I tap to pay in Nigerian stores?


Only at terminals with contactless enabled, and many terminals in Nigeria lack the hardware. Your phone also needs NFC. Look for the contactless symbol, and keep another way to pay.


### Does my Kuda, OPay, or Moniepoint card work with Google Pay?


Not at the moment. Cards from Kuda, OPay, Moniepoint, and PalmPay are not on Google's list. Check the list again later, because it can change. For dollar payments online, a virtual dollar card is another option.


### Is Google Wallet the same as Google Pay?


Not exactly. Google Wallet is the app that stores your cards, tickets, and passes. Google Pay is the payment function inside it. You install Google Wallet, add a card, and pay with Google Pay.
